speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister) moved
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: RESOURCES AND DEVELOPMENT, MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS, CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolutions:
That it is expedient to present a bill to constitute a Department of Resources and Development with a presiding minister to be appointed by commission under the Great Seal of Canada, with the duties, powers and functions as therein set out, a deputy minister to be appointed by the governor in council, and the necessary officers, clerks and employees to be appointed in the manner authorized by law, with provision also for the transfer of members of the staff of the Department of Mines and Resources or the Department of Reconstruction and Supply to the new department.
That it is expedient to present a bill to constitute a Department of Mines and Technical Surveys with a presiding minister to be appointed by commission under the Great Seal of Canada, with the duties, powers and functions as therein set out, a deputy minister to be appointed by the governor in council and the necessary officers, clerks and employees to be appointed in the manner authorized by law, with provision also for the transfer of members of the staff of the Department of Mines and Resources or the Department of Reconstruction and Supply to the new department.
That it is expedient to present a bill to constitute a Department of Citizenship and Immigration with a presiding minister to be appointed by commission under the Great Seal of Canada, with the duties, powers and functions as therein set out, a deputy minister to be appointed by the governor in council, and the necessary officers, clerks and employees to be appointed in the manner authorized by law, with provision also for the transfer of members of the staff of the Department of Mines and Resources and the Department of the Secretary of State to the new department.
He said:	I understand the Minister of
Public Works (Mr. Fournier) has discussed these three resolutions with the leaders of the various groups in the house, pointing out that they really involve only one matter and that it might be convenient if they were considered in committee at the same time. If there is no objection, I move that the Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee to consider these three integrated resolutions, dealing with the setting up of three new departments.

subtopic: RESOURCES AND DEVELOPMENT, MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS, CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext: In view of the fact that we are merging the three resolutions in order to expedite the matter, it might be well for the Prime Minister to make his statement before the Speaker leaves the chair; then we can discuss these matters in committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: RESOURCES AND DEVELOPMENT, MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS, CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext:
If that is the wish of the house, I have no objection. I thought possibly in the course of my statement some
[Mr. St. Laurent.)
questions might arise which I could answer immediately, but I can make my statement now, and the questions can be asked and answered when the house is in committee.
The main reason for legislation this session in this respect is the necessity of making some permanent provision for the functions now performed by the Department of Reconstruction and Supply. Hon. members will recall that this was one of the measures foreshadowed in the speech from the throne. It was thought at first that the Department of Reconstruction and Supply might be simply dismantled and its existing functions transferred to other departments of government, and in fact that process was under way after the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) assumed his present portfolio. Several of the functions which had appertained to the Department of Reconstruction and Supply were subsequently transferred to the Department of Trade and Commerce.
A year ago, when the present Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) was appointed, most of the remaining functions which that department had inherited from the Department of Munitions and Supply were transferred to the Department of Trade and Commerce, and the functions left in the Department of Reconstruction and Supply were largely those inherited from the original department of reconstruction which had been set up in 1944, plus ministerial responsibility for housing and for tourist activities.
It was understood when the present minister was appointed that the department was a stopgap, as it were, and that at an early day there would be a redistribution of departmental functions. When we began to give consideration to the appropriate departments to which the remaining functions of the Department of Reconstruction and Supply might be transferred, it appeared that the department which had the most closely related functions was mines and resources. That department, however, already was rather unwieldy, and the government concluded that it would not be reasonable simply to add further functions to that department, including what was becoming the heavy ministerial responsibility in respect of housing. It was then decided to redistribute the functions of the two departments in the way we felt would contribute most to efficient administration and expeditious service to the public. There were two branches of the Department of Mines and Resources each of which was obviously capable of providing the focus or nucleus for a new department, They were the mines branch and the immigration branch. As a matter of fact there had been a department of mines previously,

which in 1936 was combined with the department of the interior to become the Department of Mines and Resources.

subtopic: RESOURCES AND DEVELOPMENT, MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS, CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext: It never had a separate minister, did it?

subtopic: RESOURCES AND DEVELOPMENT, MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS, CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext:
I would not like to say, because that department went back to 1907, and I would not care to make a positive assertion about the whole of the forty-two years. As the hon. member knows, the Geology and Mines Act provided for the creation of a department of mines. That was a statute of 1907, which has never been repealed; but the sections which provided for the setting up of a separate department of mines were repealed in 1936 when the Department of Mines and Resources was created, and those functions were transferred to mines and resources at that time.
There has been a growing feeling, particularly among those interested in mining, that the importance of the mining industry and of the government's relations with that industry was such that there might well be a minister of the crown devoting most of his time to this field of mines and mining. Then, of course, there are certain surveys of a technical nature carried on by the government, in particular the geological survey, which are closely related to the development of mining. Moreover it was felt that the other technical surveys, such as geodetic, topographical and hydrographic, now administered by the Department of Mines and Resources, would be likely to be more expeditiously administered if included in the department which had the responsibility for the geological survey, and that having these together in a well-integrated department would be more likely to do away with overlapping.
In this connection it is worth noting that the union with Newfoundland added to the territory of Canada the island itself and the large area of Labrador as well, which will add considerably to the territorial scope of the activities of the proposed Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.
On more than one occasion in this house there was expressed a growing feeling that the immigration branch had very little relationship to the other activities of the Department of Mines and Resources. It was almost an orphan, perhaps in very good company but not in a company that had any special reason for being interested in its activities. The increasing importance and complexity of immigration required more attention from both the minister and the deputy minister than it was humanly possible to give to the immigration branch, included as it was with the numerous other branches of the Department of Mines and Resources. I am sure
New Departments
that many hon. members have felt that, on occasion, it took more time than appeared to them to be necessary to have matters dealt with in the immigration branch when they had to receive the personal attention of the minister or deputy minister of the Department of Mines and Resources.
It has also been apparent for some time that the relationship between the citizenship branch, under my colleague the Secretary of State, and the immigration branch, under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Mines and Resources, should be as close as possible. The citizenship branch is designed to bring to full citizenship as many as possible of those who immigrate to this country. The scope of the citizenship branch has been expanded since the passing of the citizenship act. It was felt that uniformity of policy and treatment was more likely to be achieved if one minister had the responsibility for both immigration activities and the activities pursued by this branch of the government to bring those immigrants as quickly as could reasonably be expected to full citizenship. It was felt, too, that having these two branches of administration in the one department would be more apt to avoid possible overlapping of services.
Once the decision had been reached to recommend the establishment of a Department of Citizenship and Immigration, it was considered that the minister responsible for this department should, in addition, be given the responsibility for the Indian affairs branch. I believe it is the policy of all members of the house to attempt to have the Indian affairs branch administered in such a way as to bring the original inhabitants of Canadian territory to citizenship as quickly as that can reasonably be accomplished. It was felt that it would have some psychological effect to say that these three activities dealing with human beings, and which are designed to bring those human beings to the status of full citizenship as rapidly as possible, were under the one head. Having citizenship, immigration and Indian affairs in the one department would indicate that the purpose of the activities of that department was to make Canadian citizens of those who were born here of the original inhabitants of the territory, or those who migrated to this country.
It is not intended, of course, that the hospitalization of the Indians will be transferred from the Department of National Health and Welfare to the new department. It is felt that it creates a good psychological effect to leave the impression that the health of the Indians is a matter which is of the same concern to the public as the health of those who enjoy full citizenship in Canada. Once the limits of those two departments were charted, it

New Departments
became clearer than ever that the most important remaining activities of the Department of Mines and Resources and the Department of Reconstruction and Supply, including the administration of the National Housing Act, trans-Canada highway and so forth, were concerned with a single purpose, namely, the physical development of the various aspects of our national heritage.
As those who were here at the time will remember, the purposes of post-war reconstruction were defined by my predecessor, Mr. King, when he introduced the bill to establish the reconstruction department on April 17, 1944, as involving the re-employment of nearly two million Canadians whose activities had been channelled to war activities during the last terrible war; the conversion of wartime industries to peacetime industries; the recovery of markets which had been dislocated during the war period; the restoration of railways, highways, and other capital equipment which had deteriorated during the war; the development of civil aviation; the planning of public works and services and the development of projects to provide alternative employment while wartime industries were being converted to peacetime purposes; the encouragement of new housing, both urban and rural, and the improvement of existing housing. Many of these objectives were the primary responsibility of other departments, and many of them have already been achieved.
The original reconstruction department was to be mainly concerned with co-ordinating the activities of all the departments, but it was to have a special responsibility for the planning of public projects and services, and the development of projects. Later, the responsibility for housing was transferred from the Department of Finance to the department of reconstruction. The last two responsibilities, for public projects and housing, are the main continuing responsibilities of the Department of Reconstruction and Supply. When the present minister accepted the portfolio in November, 1948, he also assumed responsibility for the encouragement and improvement of our important tourist industry. These activities-housing, and public projects and tourist promotion-will fit quite naturally into the activities to be taken over by the new Department of Resources and Development from the Department of Mines and Resources, such as jurisdiction relating to the forest resources of Canada, irrigation projects, and water-power developments not specially assigned to any other department.
I believe we must realize that the development of this country in population and in
[Mr. St. Laurent.1
utilized wealth is proceeding, and is apt to proceed. I believe we shall be making a valuable and necessary contribution to the future generation of Canadians by giving attention at once to proper forestry in Canada. This is a resource that can be renewed yearly. I was impressed by a book I read recently, entitled, "The Coming Age of Wood", by Mr. Glesinger, the chief forestry expert of the international FAO. In this book the author emphasizes, so far as it can be supported, his view that a great increase in the population of the world could still be provided with all its essential requirements if proper attention were given to the conservation and development of the forest resources, and if proper use were made of all the material that there is in a tree. According to the development of his theme, this result would be brought about not only from the utilization of the fibres in the tree, but also from the effect of good forestry on the control of the flow of rivers and streams, and on the prevention of the erosion of valuable top soil. The house will no doubt welcome the introduction of the bill, which is on the order paper at the present time, for enabling legislation to permit this government to enter into agreements with the provincial governments to assist in the development of proper forestry methods throughout the whole country.
The Department of Resources and Development would take over from the Department of Mines and Resources the national parks and various special development projects, as well as the control and management of the affairs of the Northwest Territories, the Yukon Territory and all federal crown lands not specially put under the control of other departments; and in general it would have the co-ordinating of all these activities in which the federal government can engage, either alone or in co-operation with the provinces, for the better development for the future Canada of the great natural resources with which Providence has so bountifully blessed this land.
The scope of this new Department of Resources and Development will be wide and varied. All its activities can properly be described as activities looking to the development of those resources. I can see no reason why it should not become a well-integrated department, and one in which, having all these activities, the services, skill and experience of the civil servants in one branch would be available for assistance in other branches. The broad objective of the government is to establish three departments with clearly-defined and closely-related functions and of manageable proportions.

We feel that this objective will be achieved by implementing the proposals we are now submitting.
To summarize, these departments will have the functions provided for in the Department of Mines and Resources Act, in the Geology and Mines Act, in the Department of Reconstruction Act and in the Department of Reconstruction and Supply Act. Under the bills which will be introduced, if the resolutions are adopted, the acts which I have just named will be repealed. These departments would also have the functions now in the citizenship branch of the Department of the Secretary of State. The bills would provide that they come into effect on proclamation.
It will of course take some little time after the legislation is enacted to have the proper preparations made for the sorting out of these branches; but it would be the intention, as soon as the legislation is passed, to proceed at once to the sorting out of the branches and to the setting up of three departments at as early a date as that can be done. It may be that at the outset no new minister will be appointed, but that one minister will be charged with the responsibility for some one or other of these three departments, in addition to the functions he now discharges.

subtopic: RESOURCES AND DEVELOPMENT, MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS, CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext:
I should like to make a few brief observations, Mr. Speaker, with respect to the legislation envisaged by the three resolutions which the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has described and explained.
New Departments
First of all, despite the suggestion at the conclusion of the Prime Minister's speech to the effect that this did not necessarily mean another minister of the crown-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: RESOURCES AND DEVELOPMENT, MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS, CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext: Not immediately.

subtopic: RESOURCES AND DEVELOPMENT, MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS, CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext:
-I want to make it abundantly clear that we are not setting up these departments for the purpose of having two of them administered by one minister of the crown; I think the house ought to be fully aware of that fact. A review of similar situations in the past will indicate that a department is never left on the loose for very long without some ambitious minister or new member desiring to be at the head of it.
I think we may as well realize now that we are to have another cabinet minister. I thought the Prime Minister might have cut this Gordian knot; it would have been a simple matter. What he should have said is that all these resolutions and all these changes in departments mean that we want to get a minister from Alberta, and that we want to give him a good portfolio. I am in agreement with the Prime Minister on that score, but I do not think we should describe so many circles in trying to get a minister from Alberta. Alberta deserves a minister; it has been without one for too long. I must say this, however. In the performance of his duties Hon. James A. MacKinnon, who is now in the Senate, did a magnificent job, and I would be the first one to commend him. But, as all hon. members will agree, there is a need for a minister from Alberta, and I suggest to the Prime Minister that arrangements be made for one as soon as possible, so that there may be proper parliamentary representation in the government for that ever-growing province. If there is a province in Canada that has made real progress, particularly in recent years, it is Alberta. It has made tremendous strides.

subtopic: RESOURCES AND DEVELOPMENT, MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS, CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext: Politically, too.

subtopic: RESOURCES AND DEVELOPMENT, MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS, CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext:
Yes. I know the hon. member is an expert on that, and I shall give him the field. But apart altogether from politics, because that may not be a good indication, the progress made by Alberta has been remarkable, and it should have representation in the cabinet. I do not think it is necessary, however, to take this circuitous route to get it.
When the Liberal government came into power in 1935 we had seventeen ministers of the crown. We now have twenty-one, and we are to have another, which makes twenty-two. Before the Prime Minister starts dividing up departments in order to squeeze in a man from Alberta he ought to consider the numerous

New Departments
applications he must receive every day from members of his own cabinet to be appointed to the other place. That would be an easier way to handle the Alberta situation than the cumbersome method that is being employed. I look across at the government benches and I see men who I am sure would welcome an appointment to the other place. Some of the appointments should not be delayed too long. Instead of making the cabinet bigger, it would be easier in the long run to do that and save the taxpayers a considerable amount of money; we could then have an Alberta minister without increasing the number of ministers.
Of course there is another problem. Every time a new department is set up, every time we have a new cabinet minister, inevitably parliamentary assistants start to come in. We started this in 1943. Many of the parliamentary assistants are such good men that I hesitate to say much about them, except that you can get too much of a good thing, and that is what I am attempting to advise the Prime Minister against at this time.
When the system of parliamentary assistants was instituted in 1943, we had seven. By the time we had arrived at the beginning of the last session we had crept up to twelve. I know it is down to ten now, but that is just a temporary shortage. I believe the supply is much greater than the demand, and I have no doubt the number will creep up again.
When we are speaking about cabinet ministers and parliamentary assistants, we must remember that from 1936 up to the present time we have increased the total membership of the House of Commons by seventeen 

from 245 to 262. In that time we have increased the number of parliamentary assistants and cabinet ministers by fifteen. For practically every new member added to the total membership of the house a parliamentary assistant or a cabinet minister has been added. A halt will have to be called to this, because one of these days the public will be asking: Why the necessity for so many ministers and parliamentary assistants at this particular time.
I should like to say a word about the names that are used to describe the new departments. The government must have been at a loss to find suitable names when they were making these changes. To me they are cumbersome and difficult. I was interested in what the Prime Minister said about putting the Indian affairs branch in the new Department of Citizenship and Immigration. The Indians, with their numerous and justifiable claims, will wonder whether there is some significance in their being placed in the same department as displaced persons from
[Mr. Graydon.l
abroad, because they have on occasion suggested that they were displaced persons at home. These suggested names are following the general line. As I pointed out in a previous debate, the general terminology applied to our ministries has been cumbersome and clumsy, and also confusing. I should like to impress upon the government the necessity of making the change that was suggested witih respect to "Department of External Affairs".
It is a cumbersome name, and I hope that at the next session the government will change it.
I should now like to refer to the Department of the Secretary of State. What I have to say is no reflection upon the present genial Secretary of State (Mr. Bradley), because these are not personal matters; they have to do with the departments. After all, the Secretary of State is not one of the overburdened ministers of the crown. I know that every minister feels he has too much to do, and perhaps more to do than any other minister. But there are some departments from which work could have been subtracted with a better result than from the Department of the Secretary of State. There are two or three departments that could readily be amalgamated, after a review by the government, thus avoiding an increase in the number of ministers. We are moving toward an unwieldy and cumbersome system of government when in peacetime we increase the number above that which prevailed during the war.
While this great move is being made by the government for additional help, it will at once be recognized how powerful was the argument made by some hon. members not so long ago on going into supply. They indicated that the opposition, no matter how small or large their numbers, are greatly hampered by the fact that they have not adequate facilities for research, and the like. In other words, with added parliamentary assistants, with added cabinet ministers, with heads of departments behind the ministers, the whole parliamentary debating system is loaded in favour of the government. I do not think it is quite fair; I do not think it is quite right. I am not suggesting that the opposition ought to have special favours. All I am asking is that at least the opposition be placed in a position to fulfil properly the functions which the government, parliament and the people expect it to fulfil.
In view of the complex structure of the many problems facing Canada today, there is need for specialized research and assistance in order that they may be properly debated in the house. I defy any member

or any minister of the crown, even the Prime Minister, to make an intelligent and comprehensive contribution to debates in the house without having the advantage of research. None of us has sufficient time to spend in research; the cabinet has not the time, nor have others who take prominent parts in the debates of the house. Some sort of arrangement should be made by which the opposition may be given technical assistance by way of research and the like in the preparation of their work in the house. I repeat that in my view the appointment of additional ministers is a step in the wrong direction. Changes could have been made in the cabinet, perhaps through transfer from one post to another, which would have served the purpose equally well, and would have permitted the appointment of a minister from Alberta without delay.

subtopic: RESOURCES AND DEVELOPMENT, MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS, CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, generally speaking I think the proposal made by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) for the creation of three new departments is pretty much in line with what should be done. It seems to me only logical that we should have a Department of Mines and Technical Surveys to deal with the technical side of government administration, a Department of Resources and Development to deal with the planning of our development and the use of our resources, and a Department of Citizenship and Immigration to bring both immigration and citizenship into conformity with modern conceptions. To that extent we welcome this proposal.
What I was going to say, however, was that I do not think that should involve the appointment of a new cabinet minister or the enlargement of the cabinet. I have often felt that our present departmental arrangements are based upon a conception of government administration of long ago, and that no substantial changes have been made in the last forty or fifty, or perhaps even in the last eighty years, so far as departmental divisions of power and administration are concerned.
Governmental activities are entirely different now from what they were twenty-five, thirty, forty or fifty years ago. Instead of being merely an arbitrator in the economic life of the nation, or perhaps a sort of policeman, the government is engaged in all kinds of economic and social activities. Those of us who followed the developments during the war, and in the more recent period the development of atomic energy, if I may use that as an example, realize that more and more governmental activities are being pushed-not because of the thinking of the present generation, but because of economic and social necessities.
New Departments
It seems to me that hon. members generally, and the government particularly, should direct their thoughts to the reorganization of the departments so as to meet more effectively the needs of modern economic and social environment. This is true also of the House of Commons itself. Surely our committees need some reorganization. The obligation placed upon some committees is altogether too great, while other committees never meet. A reorganization of committees of the house should be undertaken, and at the same time some thought given to the reorganization of the cabinet itself, having in mind a reallotment of power so as to meet the modern needs of the present generation.
I think it is a sound idea to give young members an opportunity to receive training in departmental administration, and I am not quite as critical as is the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) about the appointment of ministerial assistants. Already the policy of the former prime minister of bringing in young men to assist the ministers has been largely justified, in the light of the ability of those who have come forward and in some instances have subsequently assumed the responsibilities of departmental administration.
This has been going on for generations in the British parliament. When one thinks of the number of parliamentary secretaries, under-secretaries and the like who have become part and parcel of the British administrative and parliamentary system, and when one realizes that they have gradually reached the stage where the public has had confidence in them, and where a prime minister, whether new or continuing, can look around among those young men and make a selection, I think that in the interest of government efficiency the policy adopted by this government in that connection has been justified by subsequent events.
In my view the placing of matters related to immigration and citizenship under one department of Department of Citizenship and Immigration is a wise move. I was, of course, an immigrant; it is now forty years since I came to this country. It is essential that people who come here as immigrants should be not only welcomed but also taught to value the citizenship of this country, and to have an appreciation of what Canada means to them. My own view is that in every way possible we should endeavour to make our newcomers conscious of their Canadian citizenship rather than of the citizenship they once held. If we do that, we shall build up a more unified country, with less difficulty among those comprising it, so that our population, while cosmopolitan

New Departments
in its origin, may be unified in its conception of Canadian nationality, and its pride in that nationality.
I was pleased to hear the Prime Minister say that our Indian population is to be encouraged more and more to assume its place in the life of our country. It has always struck me as strange that while in New Zealand, for example, large numbers of the Maoris have attained high office in the army and become members of parliament, and so on, and have thus played a great part in the public life of New Zealand, in Canada in relation to the Indians we have had very few instances of the kind. One recalls that many who in law have made real contributions to the life of this country-and there comes to my mind the name of a chief justice of Saskatchewan of a few years ago-in the church, in education and in other fields of endeavour, have had at least a fairly substantial admixture of Indian blood. Therefore it seems to me there is no reason why our Indian population should not be encouraged to take an active part in Canadian public affairs.
I was also interested to hear the Prime Minister speak of conservation, and his conception thereof in relation to the new departments that were being set up and their responsibility in that regard. I think we must give more consideration to this question than we have over the last number of years. I have read, for example, about this beautiful Ottawa valley, where the parliament buildings are situated, once upon a time having great forests of white pine which were cut down, shipped down the Ottawa river to the St. Lawrence and thence across the seas to provide masts for the great sailing ships of other days. Today you can drive from one end of the Ottawa valley to the other and you will have difficulty in finding stands of white pine of any size. They have gone, and their place has been taken by small scrub trees suitable only for firewood or pulpwood.
What is true of this valley is true of many parts of this country. In British Columbia I have seen great logs coming out of the forests on slings, the cutting down of trees and the accumulation of slash that remain. The wastefulness of generations gone by and of our generation is something for which posterity will condemn us. It is up to us to see to it that we provide for conservation.
I remember a short time ago I was driving through a section of Canada a newcomer to this country, from one of the Baltic states. I was asked why it was that there were no trees, why there were only stumps, and why it was that nothing grew here. I explained

that the trees had been cut down and nothing had been done to replace them. This person said to me: "For many years that has not been permitted in my country; the cutting of the trees is entirely under the supervision and control of the government". That is particularly true in countries such as Norway and Sweden. I know the difficulty. Whenever any province of Canada endeavours to put into effect a forest conservation policy, the outcry is made that they are interfering with so-called private enterprise. No matter whether we believe in private enterprise or some other sort of enterprise, one thing we owe to our own and to future generations is that there shall not be private exploitation and the denuding of our forest lands and our other resources in the interests merely of the present generation. In Norway, Sweden and the Baltic states forest conservation policies have been in effect for years.
The same applies of course to soils. I was born in a part of Great Britain where the land has been farmed for more than two thousand years, ever since the Phoenicians first came to the shores of the British isles. During the whole of that time crops have been reaped, and today the cropping of that same soil produces far better results than much of the newer soil of Canada. Soil conservation is something we should consider more than we have considered it in the past.
If the reorganization of departments foreshadows a more intelligent policy of dealing with our minority races, our forests and our soil, then it is to be welcomed. I am not convinced, however, as the hon. member for Peel is not convinced, that it is an extension of the number of cabinet ministers or the number of departments that is necessary. While welcoming the new divisions, I rather believe that the government should be considering the reorganization of governmental responsibilities among the cabinet ministers, and the reapportionment of administrative powers among even fewer cabinet ministers than we have today.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to add to the debate a voice from this corner of the house. While we are largely in favour of these three resolutions, believing as we do that government administration should be facilitated to the greatest possible extent in order that government may be as efficient as possible; yet we do have some diffidence as to the need for three departments. It seems to me that one of them is justified, while perhaps there is not so much reason for the other two. I believe the resolution creating a special Department of Citizenship and Immigration, and perhaps

putting Indian affairs under that department, is a good move. I agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) when he says that immigrants need to be trained in an appreciation of Canadian citizenship. Not only would the minister be responsible for the general process which takes place as one becomes a Canadian citizen, but also he would have a larger responsibility for the probationary period during which these newcomers to Canada learn something of the opportunities, freedoms and other advantages that Canada has to offer. We are very much in favour of the creation of that department.
We cannot be so enthusiastic about the necessity for the other two departments. My main reason for saying so is that, after all, the natural resources of Canada come under provincial jurisdiction. I recognize there are large areas in the Northwest Territories that geographically come under this government. I am afraid that in a good deal of the work carried on there is considerable duplication as between the government here and the government of the provinces. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has said something about forestry in the Ottawa valley. I do not know who is responsible; it seems to me that would be a provincial matter, but his remarks should be directed to those who have the responsibility. Anything that is good, of course, should be continued, but we do have to protect the expenditures of this country to some extent, though I personally am not one of those who care to scrutinize every dollar. As a matter of fact my economic philosophy is one of spending rather than conserving. I believe in spending; that is what makes the wheels of industry go round. It seems to me the philosophy of thrift has been carried to the extreme. However, that is just an aside. With the taxation system under which we are living we have to guard expenditures, because in the final analysis this government is going to make the people pay for everything that is done.
I realize the significance of what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has said in respect to the economic and social life of a nation assuming greater and perhaps more important proportions, with the result that someone has to take charge somewhere. Thus it devolves upon the government to extend its administration, which might be the natural thing to expect. But I do not know that I altogether agree with that, for this reason. I believe there is a tendency among nations to build up and create a bureaucracy to do things for people which by their very nature, being
New Departments
human beings, they should be able to do for themselves. I believe the tendency toward bureaucracy exists because we have certain false conceptions with respect to society at large. Governments increase their number; their administration increases in machinery and personnel in the process of building up this bureaucracy. But the human race does not change. How does this all come about? I wonder if we have ever thought of that. Human nature does not change; it is the same as it always has been. We still wear hats of the same size; we still think with the same brains; we still eat three meals a day; we still sleep in beds; we still breathe the air; we get up in the morning about the same time; we go to bed perhaps a little later than our predecessors did. Human nature is the same; man is a free moral agent, and so on. Where does the difference come in? I think the difference arises from the fact that somehow or other there is a design somewhere to render men less free; and believe me, the more government increases-it is government here, government there, government somewhere else-the more that design will become clear. People talk in terms of government, government, government. Well, the more you talk in terms of government the less you can talk in terms of men being free. It might be well for us to reflect a little on this bit of philosophy.
Let me tell you what I think should be done if there is to be any increase at all in services. I believe the ordinary member of parliament should be given additional help. If government administration increases, or if there is to be an increase in administrative machinery, that must apply also to members of parliament. I am sure I speak for many hon. members. I happen to sit here at a sort of forty-five degree angle from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and sometimes I have occasion to look under his desk. I do not think he wears an oversize shoe, but I do not know how he finds a place for his feet among all the books and papers he brings down here and piles under his desk. Perhaps his personal staff should be increased by an extra messenger to carry down his books.
That is just a little sidelight, of course. Let us look at the tremendous machinery involved in carrying on the government. Let us look at the government reports that come to our desks. No member of parliament is able to read them all; there are not enough hours in the day. No member of parliament could read fast enough to be able to read everything that comes to his desk, even if he were to read for twenty-four hours a day.

New Departments
Here we have the Department of External Affairs, a tremendously responsible department these days, through which we have our connection with the United Nations. Foreign relations is a matter that is becoming more and more important. How much does the average member of parliament know about foreign relations? I am casting no reflection upon members of the house as such, but it is almost impossible to read everything that is issued by the United Nations, coming to us through the external affairs department, and become expert in those matters in addition to looking after our other work.
If the government finds that its increasing responsibilities are such as to require a greater number of ministers and staff and administrative machinery, how much more does that apply to members of parliament. Here we are packed up in little offices. We should have more office space; we should have special and personal research men who can go into these things and boil our work down for us, so that the stature of this house would be raised in the eyes of the public who sit in these galleries. It may be that there are not so many in the galleries this morning because I am speaking; but I believe the real reason why more people do not frequent parliament is that most people believe this is a pretty dull place. It should not be so, and it would not be so if each member of parliament had an adequate staff. I do not mean the mere sharing of a secretary; I mean a research man. I am thinking of someone who could give information about the various subjects taken up in the house, so that the member of parliament could study legislation which at times is very intricate. I sat in the house during the debate on the measures to abolish appeals to the privy council, the revision of the constitution' and the Combines Investigation Act; they were extremely involved. The members of the legal profession had quite a tournament at that time.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are just leaning over to tell me to come to order because I am straying from the subject. I shall return to the subject, but I am conscious of the fact that I cannot do all my work and be as expert as I should like to be because the government has not seen fit to give us adequate staff.
I am heartily in sympathy with the resolution respecting citizenship and immigration, but I think the other two-oh, we are not going to hold it up, because it is not that important-could well be put together.

There are one or two observations, Mr. Speaker, which I had intended to make in committee, but which might be made at this time.
We had a statement from the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) which recalled to my mind a statement about the Prime Minister made by an old friend of his. It concerned the days when the Prime Minister used to appear in court. This man said the Prime Minister really did not have to argue; he just stated the facts of his case but stated them so persuasively that that ended the matter. I believe we have to be on guard against the persuasiveness and charm of the Prime Minister. When he tells us these things, it almost sounds as if they proved themselves.
I should like to make one or two comments which are really a sort of footnote to what the member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) said. The problem of the Prime Minister with respect to Alberta was clearly explained by the member for Peel, and he referred also to the more general problem of the Prime Minister with a huge and successful following who naturally feel they would like to profit in various ways from their electoral success. The Prime Minister, being what he is, finds himself sympathetic to them. His position reminds me of a few lines written by that great philosopher, W. S. Gilbert, who put his philosophy in rhymes which are easy to remember. The lines which I shall read, I suggest, depict in some fashion the position in which the Prime Minister finds himself at the moment:
There lived a king, as I've been told,
In the wonder-working days of old,
When hearts were twice as good as gold,
And1 twenty times as mellow.
Then, it continues:
He wished all men as rich as he (And he was rich as rich could be);
So to the top of every tree Promoted everybody.
The Prime Minister, as the member for Peel has already indicated, is in a quandary, in that he would like to make as many appointments as possible that would be pleasant to those who receive them.
It was perhaps a little unfortunate that this additional government expenditure should have been announced this morning, after we had heard from the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) that he was almost in a position to cut down the number of his staff by some thousands. Of course the Minister of National Revenue comes from Queen's university, and I am prepared to believe that, in many ways, he is in a

class by himself. Nevertheless I say it is a little disappointing, when we seemed to be in sight of a little economy, to be subjected to a cold douche the next morning. We find that, instead of economy, there is going to be a great deal of expenditure.
It is never popular to talk about economy.
I do not hold myself out as any authority, but I should like to read a word or two from the Winnipeg Free Press, to which I understand the government gives ear from time to time. Actually it is written about the trade situation, but there are a few words here which I think apply. The Free Press says this:
-Canada cannot afford to undertake many of the expensive projects which seemed possible before but are now clearly beyond our means.
This, of course, is not one of the projects which the Free Press had in mind-at least I do not think it was. Nevertheless it seems to me that economy is economy, and extravagance is extravagance. If in fact we are setting up a department which is not necessary-and I shall come to that in a moment- then we are in fact extravagant.
I remember a wise remark made by the head of a corporation whom I heard speaking to one of his colleagues who was proposing to add a new department to his firm. He said: "Now, that may be necessary, but do not fool yourself as to what you are doing; you are setting up a new kingdom, and the king will want to have as many subjects as possible." That is true. If it is true in business, where one has the acid test of the profit and loss account, how much truer is it in the public service, where there is no such test, and where the sky is the limit.
I am only going to say a word or two about the departments. I do not think anyone will quarrel about what the Prime Minister said as to the need for dealing with the various matters to which he referred. We hold up both hands for that. It was interesting to hear the Prime Minister say that at one time the dismantling of the Department of Reconstruction and Supply had been considered. As I understood him, he gave an interesting reason for that when he said it had been thought that when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) left reconstruction and supply to go to trade and commerce, he would take many of his functions with him. That, of course, is quite commendable, but I do not intend to pursue it further. I do wish to say that I am glad the Department of Reconstruction and Supply was not dismantled, and we all cordially approve of the minister who was appointed to it.
New Departments
This point is still left, however, as the hon. member for Peel has already indicated: There are three or four departments, such as defence, national revenue and finance, which have under their control a far wider range of matters, a far more impressive amount of business, than this new department will have. I entirely agree with what the member for Peel said about the Secretary of State. Surely part of this could have been left with him. If in the Department of National Defence there is this tremendous range of business which is dealt with by one minister with deputies, it cannot be suggested that these matters could not have been dealt with in the same way.
I have no desire to take more time than I have. The only point I want to make is that in my opinion this is an unnecessary extravagance. It could have been dealt with another way. However pleasant it may be to elevate a new person to the stature of a minister, what we are doing is setting up a kingdom which will eventually cost this country-and I make a conservative estimate -several tens of thousands of dollars per year.

Mr. Speaker, I have always felt that the Department of Mines and Resources should have a thorough psychoanalysis. I have always felt the name was a misnomer, because the department has little to do with either mines or resources. I have often tried to ascertain what the functions of the department are. The estimates of the department come to the house, generally, as those of a minister who has very little to do with the technical matters that are supposed to be handled by it, and the minister is looked upon in the house as just another supernumerary rendering an annual report. I have always felt that this department should have some kind of tightening up. Whether this is the proper way to do it or not, I am not prepared to say.
The arguments that new departments and new ministerial posts are not necessary do not impress me greatly, because anyone who thinks in those terms has not been keeping abreast of the times. You cannot compare the Canada of 1949 with the Canada of even 1939. We are living in a completely different age. The argument against a ministry of trade and commerce is ridiculous, because practically all trade on an international scale today is done between government and government, and it is necessary to have a department for that purpose. Our internal markets also are largely regulated by the government. Where would the apple growers, the wheat growers or the fish industry be if

New Departments
it were not for the fact that a government board is buying up their surpluses and marketing them on an international scale? Whether we like it or not, that is the development; if we are to keep up to date, business will have to be done in that way.
The government is in business, whether some people like it or not. I should like to bring to the attention of the house the extent to which the present Minister of Trade and Commerce has taken the government into business, and rightly so. In the last three or four weeks he has been kicked around in this house a good deal, but I think he has done an excellent job in the field of protecting certain essential services in this country for the people of Canada. I have in mind Trans-Canada Air Lines for example. I do not think we would have T.C.A. if it were not for the fact that we had in the Minister of Trade and Commerce a fairly stubborn person who believed that we should have it. The radio is another example. The measure of public control is, I think, largely due to his activities. Then there is the Polymer Corporation. We are all proud of it. It has done an excellent job. It was thrown together when its creation was absolutely essential. Then there is Canadian Arsenals, and there are other examples that I could mention. I think the minister did an excellent job in that respect.
In order to supervise and properly control these activities, a department is necessary with someone in charge of it who really understands the situation. My only quarrel with the three resolutions that are now before us is this. For example, in the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, when a minister is appointed, I do not think the appointment should be made on a political basis; neither do I think that it should be made on a geographical basis. I am not particularly concerned about whether Nova Scotia has a minister or not, or whether Alberta has one or not. But I am anxious that the minister who is appointed to that portfolio shall have the qualifications necessary for proper supervision of the department's activities. The same observation applies with regard to the Department of Resources and Development. As to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, it can be handled by anyone who can read and write. The other departments, however, are technical departments.
I should like to direct the minister's thoughts to another aspect of the situation with regard to the first two departments I have just mentioned. Mines and technical surveys are matters that are dealt with by the provincial governments also. The provincial governments have complete control

over whatever minerals may be discovered. They also have a large measure of control in the granting of charters for any development that may take place as a result of these technical surveys. To what extent are we duplicating, federally, the work that is done by the provinces? I have checked on this business to some extent with regard to technical surveys, particularly as to minerals. One reason why I am glad to see that whole subject now departmentalized under some responsible person is this: as far back in the past as research has been carried on by the Department of Mines and Resources, it has served little purpose. I will mention only one aspect of their work-for example, Labrador and Ungava ore. I am informed that reports had been locked in the vaults of the federal department since 1896. Nothing was done about them until some prospector staggered over some ore and thought there was something there; then a survey was made and the archives gone into. There is no use in spending a great deal of money in carrying on that kind of work unless we are going to do something about it. I trust that under the new set-up something may be done about it.
The same thing applies to the Department of Resources and Development, having to do with a matter which also is in the hands of the provincial governments. Unless the federal government are going to enact some legislation whereby their surveys and the development of their resources is to be carried on on a national scale in co-operation with the provinces, it is just a waste of time to set up federal departments and place large staffs in them if nothing is done about the surveys made and the resources discovered. This is something upon which we must make up our minds. I hope that in the future we shall have a minister in charge of these departments who has the tenacity of purpose which the Minister of Trade and Commerce has shown. On occasions he may have shown bad judgment, but I think that any mistakes he has made were honest mistakes. To me at least, as a member of this house for the last ten years, he has demonstrated that he is the kind of person who wants to do something about the matters that he may be administering. I trust that we may have men like him in these two particular departments.
My main purpose in rising was to say that we must not be unmindful of the fact that, with regard to both of these departments, we run into the provincial governments. We should not be duplicating their work. If ministers are appointed, they should have the technical qualifications to carry on the work of the departments and to do it

properly. A minister may be placed in an extremely awkward position. Let us suppose that he is Minister of National Defence. There are many technical problems to be handled and many things that he must know something about. Suppose you bring in somebody from Alberta just because he is from Alberta. He may be a farmer, and yet you bring him to Ottawa and make him Minister of National Defence. What respect has his department for him? He is just wandering around there like a ship without a rudder.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak very briefly, because the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) and others have given expression to some of my views; but I do want to say that I am pleased in the first place to support these resolutions. Because of the explanations given to us this morning by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) I think the proposals are logical and necessary.
New Departments
It has been my experience that many adult Canadians are confused about the functions of certain departments of the federal government. The division of the departments and the naming of them in this way will dissipate some of that confusion. I am of the opinion that the more people we can get interested in the national government, the more people we can have in the country who have an understanding of the functions of the departments of the national government, the stronger our democracy will be.
There has been some reference to the appointment of further ministers. I support the remarks made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. We are a rapidly expanding and growing country, and the functions of government are rapidly expanding. I am all for appointing ministers who are required to carry out efficiently the work of these expanding and increasing departments.
With reference to the establishment of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, the new title is an improvement. As the Prime Minister said, our mines are very important to the federal government, and there is a necessity for co-ordination of the activities of the federal government with the activities of the provincial governments, particularly with regard to the conservation of natural resources, which several speakers have mentioned. In the department as now proposed we will have the majority of the technical staff, I presume, concerned with surveys and dealing with similar problems. There is a staff that is dealing with surveys in the Columbia river, the geological surveys and so on. It is a logical arrangement for that department.
When we come to the establishment of the Department of Resources and Development, of necessity an active minister will have to be appointed to that portfolio. I am all for it, Mr. Speaker, because I believe that if we are to develop our housing program, which is so necessary in this country, our trans-Canada highway system and our country generally, and if the dominion government is to support the development of Canada to the extent that will be required in the years ahead, it will be a full-time job for any efficient minister.
With respect to the establishment of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, I am pleased to see it now, because we have to expand the functions of the department in a logical way. The previous department had to do with natural resources and development. As the Prime Minister said, this department will be primarily concerned with human resources. I think the establishment.

New Departments
of a department under which immigration, citizenship and the care of Indian affairs comes under one branch is logical, and I am sure it will appeal to a large section of the country.
Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I want to make a reference to parliamentary assistants. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) criticized the number of parliamentary assistants that this government has appointed. Personally I am pleased to know that this government is appointing parliamentary assistants. I say that because of my personal experience in this house. They perform a very necessary function. In the first place, it seems only reasonable to provide an opportunity for, shall I say, the brighter and coming young men of the house to be trained in departmental activities with the possibility of being appointed cabinet ministers in the future. I think also that parliamentary assistants are a necessary link between busy cabinet ministers and their officials. They are a necessary link between busy members of parliament and the ministers' officials. From my experience I have found that the parliamentary assistants perform a useful function in this house for members of parliament. I want particularly to mention two that I have had a good deal to do with. In the first instance, I had numerous problems brought to my attention that concerned the Department of Reconstruction and Supply, not during the last twelve months but during the immediate post-war period. I must say that on numerous occasions I found the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply most helpful.
Now, sir, I say this, though I differ from the hon. member politically. So far as British Columbia is concerned we are fortunate that the Minister of Finance has for his parliamentary assistant a man of the calibre of the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair). On occasions I have had to bring to his notice problems from my constituency-because my constituents are a very alert and active people. I have found the hon. member most helpful and cooperative, and most willing on all occasions to do what he could to find a satisfactory solution to the problems that I brought to his department through him.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I simply say this. The final success, the basic success of this reorganization, depends to a great extent not only upon the ministers appointed but on the calibre of the deputy ministers appointed to assist in these departments. I do hope that in this reorganization of the departments the government will give serious
[Mr. Herridge.l
consideration to the appointment as deputy ministers of the best men that they can obtain.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word or two before the measure is finally carried. I believe that the move of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), to add to the administrative machinery which will be at his disposal, is sound. It is true, as a number of hon. members have already said, that we need to increase such machinery as the complexity of the lives of our times develops. It must be borne in mind, however, that each department must be carefully instructed to recognize that it is not its function to step into the work which is already being done by the provinces. It must be definitely understood by every cabinet minister that his prime function is that of leadership. He should never get the idea that he is a driver or necessarily a supplanter. One of his main functions is to supply the finance to those who are already engaged in carrying on the work which falls naturally under his department. Not only should he supply finance, but he should supply also technical knowledge, in so far as the dominion has it at its disposal in greater abundance than the provincial governments can have. He should provide for co-ordination among the provinces.
Up to the present time too little realization of that sort of thing has been in evidence. This country is unique in that it now consists of ten countries. If any one of the provinces of this dominion were in Europe it would be a nation with a nation's problems, a nation's capacities and a nation's resources. One of the main tasks of the minister is to bring the activities of these ten provinces into co-ordination, so that there will be no conflict among them, such as has all too frequently developed in times past. I hope the Prime Minister will take care to brief these new men adequately in this respect.
May I revert for a moment to the matter of finance? Let us take the question of Indian affairs. Busy as has been the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Gibson) in the years immediately past, he has had plenty of time, I believe, to supervise the Indians affairs branch to such an extent as to enable him to know pretty well what ought to be done for the Indians. The first has to do with the distribution of the various branches. In the present Department of Mines and Resources there is a branch known as mines, forests and scientific services. Apparently it is to be broken up and some of the sections of the branch allotted to the new Department of Resources and Development while others go to the new Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. For example, there are the following branches: the bureau of mines, the dominion forest service, the eastern rockies forest conservation board, the geological survey of Canada, the surveys and mapping bureau, the dominion water and power bureau, the geographical bureau, the national museum of Canada, and the dominion observatories.
Then there are also certain branches which, while they are under the Minister of Trade and Commerce at the present time, would appear to have their proper place in one or the other of the two new departments. One is the dominion coal board, which, it would seem, should be in the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. Then there are the national research council, the atomic energy control board and Canadian Arsenals Limited. Can the Prime Minister tell us just how these different sections of the service are to be allotted?	'

Each of these branches will have several hundred employees. subtopic: AMENDMENT OF DOMINION-PROVINCIAL TAX RENTAL AGREEMENTS ACT, 1947   INCOME TAX
speechtext:
This resolution seeks authority to introduce a short bill to amend the

Dominion-Provincial Tax Rental Agreements Act of 1947. The amending bill will refer to only one section in the act, section 7, under which the federal government and the provinces agreed, in respect of those public utilities engaged in generating or distributing electrical energy, gas or steam, that half the federal corporation tax received from them should be returned to the provincial governments.
According to section 7 there should be deducted from the provinces' half share any increase in royalties or licences which the provinces charged to the power companies after January 1, 1947, when these agreements came into effect, or any new royalties, taxes, or rentals which were imposed on the companies after January 1, 1947, and any taxes levied directly by the provinces on those power companies. Exempt, however, was the five per cent corporation tax which the federal government collects for the provinces under the dominion-provincial taxation agreement. No provision was made, however, to extend that provision to the corporation taxes levied by the provinces which had not signed the agreement. One of the clauses of the amending bill will permit the provinces who did not sign the agreement to be given credit for an equivalent amount of five per cent, so that the deduction will be made to the extent that the provincial corporation tax exceeds the five per cent cent levied by the signing provinces.
In other words, this will be a considerable benefit to the two provinces which did not sign. It will give to them the same benefits as those received by the signing provinces.
The second amendment refers to section 7 also, subsection 4. It was intended to apply this special concession only to those companies engaged in the distribution of power to the public. It was not intended to cover, for example, large industrial corporations such as a smelting company or pulp and paper company which had a wholly-owned power company as a subsidiary selling its power output entirely to the parent company. That was regarded as a normal corporation whose corporation tax would go direct to the federal government. Subsequently it was found that there are public utility corporations in this country which have a somewhat similar set-up under which one subsidiary actually generates the power and the parent company or another subsidiary sells the power to the public. Under the wording of subsection 4 the taxes from these subsidiaries would not be shared by the provinces. It was felt that was unfair, so subsection 4 of section 7 is being changed so that the provinces will receive five per
Tax Agreements
cent of the tax collected from either the subsidiary or the parent company, so long as it is engaged in selling or distributing power to the public.
The third part of the bill provides for returns and special information necessary for the proper administration of the section, and provides for the extension of this measure to cover the province of Newfoundland.

speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 143, to amend the Export and Import Permits Act.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. J. Mcllrailh (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND LIFE OF ACT UNTIL JULY 31, 1951
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that the Export and Import Permits Act was enacted in 1947. It was amended in 1948. Section 14 of the amending act provided that the act would expire on the 31st of March, 1950. The present bill seeks an extension of the act until July 31, 1951. The bill was introduced in the Senate and was considered at some length by the banking and commerce committee of the other place.
I might give a short explanation as to the reason for the choice of the date, July 31, 1951. The bill, as introduced in the Senate, provided for an extension of two years. When it was discussed in committee there a question arose about granting an extension for one year. It became evident in the discussion of that point that an extension for one year only-that is, an extension to March 31, 1951-would necessitate a further amending bill in the next session of parliament. It was thought that difficulty could be advantageously overcome by making the time of expiry of the act July 31, 1951, so that if it were desired again to extend the act the amending bill would not have to be brought in until the second session from the present one.
Originally the main purpose of controlling exports under the act was to ensure that commodities in short supply were available for domestic consumption. To a limited but constantly diminishing extent this purpose is still valid, particularly in the field of building products, if we are to maintain the high level of construction in this country. It is apparent now that the main purpose of the bill is that having to do with strategic considerations, and that is the main reason for the export permits at the present time.
It is essential that the government be responsible for the destinations to which arms, munitions, implements of war, atomic energy materials and other materials of like nature are shipped, and that is the main purpose of export control at the present time.
It will be noted that in the earlier years of the act there were some 542 items under export control. At the present time there are 137 items under export control. I might say that in effect the number of items is really considerably less than that because included

Export and Import Permits in the list are items that we normally do not produce in this country for export. They are of a kind that we import from the United States. Because of their strategic importance I think it is apparent to all hon. members that we would not wish to have them other than under export control, even although we do not produce them ourselves. An excellent example of the type of item I am talking about in that category is carbon black. It is not produced in this country, and yet it is included under export control to ensure that United States carbon black is not exported from this country.
With respect to continuing the authority for import control, the list has been reduced from 67 items under control to 5. It is necessary mainly because of our international commitments. An example of that is tin under the combined tin allocation committee, and rice under the food and agriculture organization.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND LIFE OF ACT UNTIL JULY 31, 1951
speechtext: What were the other three?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND LIFE OF ACT UNTIL JULY 31, 1951

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved
