speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 133, respecting the application of a national trade mark to commodities and respecting the true description of commodities.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO COMMODITIES
speechtext: Would the minister make a statement?

speakeroldname: Mr. G. J. Mcllrailh (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: APPLICATION TO COMMODITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill respecting the application of a national trade mark to commodities and respecting the true description of commodities was introduced in the Senate at the last session of the 20th parliament. It was dealt with by the banking and commerce committee of the Senate at that time, at considerable length. Some slight amendments were made in the bill as introduced. It was then passed by the Senate through all stages, and was on the order paper in this house when parliament dissolved.
National Trade Mark
It was reintroduced at this session in the Senate in precisely the form in which it had been passed by the Senate at the previous session. The bill has been considered and passed by the Senate without further amendment. It was referred to their committee on banking and commerce at this session, but required to be dealt with only briefly.
The bill itself relates to three subjects, the first of which is the use of the words "Canada standard" or the initials "C.S." as the national trade-mark, following the establishment of commodity standards; secondly, the accurate labelling of commodities; and, thirdly, it provides for the repeal of the Dominion Trade and Industry Commission Act of 1935.
Hon. members will recall that an attempt was made to deal with the subject matter of this bill with the passing of the Dominion Trade and Industry Commission Act in 1935. That act dealt with other matters which are unrelated to the present bill. However, the provisions of the Dominion Trade and Industry Commission Act which related to the national trade-mark, the establishment of commodity standards and true labelling were transferred to the Department of Trade and Commerce in March, 1947.
Experience has shown that the legislation is defective and unsatisfactory for the purpose originally intended. I will refer to these defects in dealing with the particular subjects contained in the bill. The new bill provides a basically new approach to the problems involved and will establish a framework within which these problems can be administered.
There is active business interest in this type of legislation. This is evidenced by the fact that a large number of requests have been received by the Department of Trade and Commerce from manufacturers, distributors, or consumer organizations for the issue of regulations, either with respect to the use of the national trade-mark or to true labelling. Applications have been put forward for the right to use the national trade-mark, but the greater number of the more pressing requests deal with commodities in regard to which more adequate labelling safeguards are desired. I may say that the issue of regulations in response to the requests that are now in hand has been held up by the department, in some cases because the investigational work required has not been completed, but also on the more important ground that the existing legislation has certain defects and does not provide adequate safeguards.
It is not considered that there will be a very rapid development or growth along the

National Trade Mark
development of the use of the national trademark. Indeed, it is desirable that this be so, in view of the fact, as hon. members will appreciate, that great care and thorough investigation of each application must be made before the right to use the national trade-mark on any product is granted. It is believed that there will be a real advantage to both the domestic and the export trade in the voluntary adoption by Canadian firms of the use of the national trade-mark under conditions that will properly safeguard the quality of the goods to which the mark is applied.
It should be clearly understood that the use of the national trade-mark by any industrial or commercial firm is wholly voluntary. It is not intended in any way to supersede or interfere with the use of privately owned trade marks, which have been long established or widely known, and represent assets of great value to the individual firms or companies to which they belong. If, however, any firm or company wishes to make use of the national trade-mark, it may do so only on the condition that its product conforms with an approved specification or standard. The extent to which its use will increase depends completely upon the extent to which business firms desire to have a national mark used on their products.
Under the old Dominion Trade and Industry Commission Act, the minister had the power to regulate the manner of using the mark, but he had no power to prescribe the terms and conditions of use. Further the governor in council had no authority over the national trade-mark. It is felt that all regulations governing the manner of using the national trade-mark, and prescribing the terms and conditions of its use, should be those of the governor in council instead of the minister as it was in the old act. These changes are effected by the present bill.
Further, under the existing legislation, once the right to use the mark had been granted there was no provision whatever for cancelling or withdrawing the right to use it if the right was abused. Under the present bill the governor in council is enabled to make regulations prescribing the circumstances in which the right of any person to affix the national trade-mark to any commodity or container may be either terminated or suspended. The importance of this safeguard will, I think, be self-evident. The potential value of the national trade-mark lies in its recognition in both domestic and export trade as a virtual guarantee of quality.
The establishment of commodity standards is a corollary to the establishment of the

national trade-mark. Under the old legislation mandatory standards or specifications may be set up for any commodities, regardless of whether or not it is intended that the national trade-mark be applied to them. In this respect the bill we are now considering makes an important change. The authority to establish a standard or specification for any commodity applies only in the case of products on which the right to use the national trade mark is being sought. Consequently, the standard or specification that may be established for any given product will be mandatory only on those firms applying the national trade-mark to such projects. There will therefore be no compulsory specification or standard that must be observed by firms which are not making use of the national trade-mark.
With respect to the second main part of the bill, the true description of labelling of commodities, it will be noted that the provisions of the present bill are not as wide as those of the existing legislation. In the Dominion Trade and Industry Commission Act there is power to compel descriptive labelling virtually without restriction. The regulations under the new bill will be mandatory only in the sense that if goods are described on labels they must be labelled accurately and in a manner that avoids public deception. The principal point to be emphasized in this connection is that regulations can only prescribe the manner of labelling if goods are labelled for the purpose of indicating the material content or quality of the commodity or the size or contents by weight or measure of the package or container.
If any individual manufacturer wishes to put out a product without marking or labelling or describing it in advertising for the above purposes, he may still do so. If he does label it, descriptively, for any of these purposes he must label it accurately. The purpose of the bill may be simply stated as follows: In establishing a national trade-mark, it is proposed that this shall be on a voluntary basis only, and the necessity of complying with commodity standards affects only those manufacturers or others who desire to use the national trade-mark. Where manufacturers descriptively label any commodity or container, it must be labelled accurately to prevent public deception.
I might add that when the bill was in committee in the other place there was a rather thorough examination of it, and representations were heard from the retail federation of Canada, the Canadian Manufacturers Association and the Canadian association of consumers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as to this measure I think I can safely say that I thought I was in thorough agreement with the broad principles of the bill, but after listening to the parliamentary assistant's description of it I do not know whether or not I am. We will not argue the fact that we should have a high standard of quality for any goods to be sold in Canada or to be exported. With that proposition we are in agreement. There is also no argument as to the true labelling of goods, but when the parliamentary assistant says that no compulsion is provided in the bill for the labelling of goods for export, I do not know whether I can go quite that far. I think probably there should be some compulsion whereby exporters of goods from Canada would have to meet certain requirements as to standards of quality and these other things. We are all seriously interested in the quality of goods exported from this country, because in order to hold our markets we must see that the quality is such that it will meet the demands of consumers in these countries.
The parliamentary assistant did not say what products the bill would deal with. I am going to say very little, as a matter of fact, but I want to look at the question from the standpoint of agriculture. If the bill has anything to do with agricultural products I want to say a few words about it. We are dependent on export business for the disposition of practically all our agricultural products. In order to secure that export business we must produce a quality that is in demand in the countries to which we sell. If we do not do so, we cannot expect to get the business.
So far as agricultural products are concerned, I may say quite frankly that I do not like the words "Canada standard" or the letters "C.S." The letters "C.S." might mean anything. The words "Canada standard", in my opinion, would mean quite ordinary or average. We certainly do not want products being exported from Canada marked with words that mean no more than ordinary or average. That is particularly so in the case of canned products. They are now graded, and the lowest quality of canned products is referred to as the standard grade. The word "standard" implies that the products are of average or ordinary quality. I do not think it is good enough for us to use such words as a Canadian trade-mark for goods that are being exported or that are being sold in the domestic market. I do not know what other word I would use, and I would not want to suggest one. Surely there should be some better word than "standard". Even though this bill has passed through all stages in the other place, I believe the government should 4578-1-I47J

give us an undertaking that it will be sent to an appropriate committee of this house to be further discussed and studied before it passes this chamber.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO COMMODITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support this measure which is to replace sections 16 to 19 of the Dominion Trade and Industry Commission Act of 1935, which is repealed by section 9 of this bill. I believe this is a good move. I was very glad to hear the parliamentary assistant say the government intends to adopt a new approach to this problem. The act apparently has been inoperative for years, and I am glad to see some evidence that it is the intention of the government to develop this type of legislation.
Before proceeding with my remarks let me say that after reading the trade and industry act of 1935 and knowing the situation in regard to the enforcement of legislation of this kind, I fully appreciate that the machinery and procedures have to be developed rather slowly, and as the result of producer and consumer support. Up to the present time we have done very little in Canada along these lines, as compared to what has been done in the United States. There, through the activities of the federal trade commission, a great deal has been done to develop national standards and the true labelling of commodities. This, I think, is evidenced by the number of investigations and prosecutions that have been conducted by the federal trade commission in recent years.
I understand that originally the federal trade commission of the United States was set up to stop unfair practices in competition and to protect the trade rather than the public. After some years of experience this was found most ineffective, and changes had to be considered.
It was not until 1938 that the United States government legally recognized the need for protecting the public as well as business interests; and I presume that in our legislation there is to be protection for the public as well as for business. This change came about in the United States as a result of the dispute between the federal trade commission and the manufacturers of a weight-reducing remedy which was found to be injurious to health. That company won its case before the supreme court of the United States on the ground that while the weight-reducing remedy might have been injurious to many customers, it never hurt a competitor. Since claims made by the competitors were equally false according to the law, this hair-splitting decision was technically correct, and I understand that was the cause of a new approach

National Trade Mark
to the problem by the commission. The court ruling in that case, which prevented the federal trade commission from proceeding against one manufacturer because all in that field were dishonest, showed the absurdity of the situation and the need for some change in the law.
As a result of that decision the Wheeler-Lee amendment was passed giving the federal trade commission power to act in the public interest as well as in the interests of business. The adoption of this amendment had a great effect upon the advertising and labelling of commodities in the United States. Since that time the commission has done a great deal of work in this connection. According to the figures I have been able to obtain, last year its staff examined some half million advertisements in newspapers, magazines and other periodicals, of which number some 25,000 were noted as containing representations apparently false or misleading. In addition over a million radio continuities were examined, and some 20,000 violations of the law were determined by the federal trade commission. As far as I can discover, during the same period of time in Canada only one violation of the law was dealt with, as compared with more than 20,000 violations in the United States.
This action in the United States was supported by many newspapers, and I mention this because I think it only right to give credit where credit is due. The Christian Science Monitor has been a great advocate of the setting up of fair standards for the manufacture of goods, and the true labelling of those goods in that country, and has consistently supported the efforts of the government in that direction. It was the first national newspaper to emphasize the harmful effect of false advertising on all mankind, and to reject such advertising for this reason rather than because it was damaging honest business.
At this point I should like to say that when this legislation is passed and the government begins to develop its procedures and to gain experience in administration, I trust the newspapers and magazines of this country will give similar support to all measures taken to improve standards and bring about true labelling. In Canada investigations and prosecutions concerning manufacturing and labelling have been far fewer than in the United States, except with regard to the inspection of primary and farm commodities, those commodities which provide the purchaser in the first instance with greater opportunity to know whether he or she has obtained the goods desired. The housewife knows she is purchasing beef. It may be a bit tougher than she anticipates; it might be
[Mr. Herrldge.l
B instead of A, but she knows it is beef. The same can be said about pork, and the same can be said about lumber. A man knows he is purchasing lumber. He may not be certain of the grade, but at least he can tell that it is lumber. When it comes to bottled or canned commodities, however, very often the purchaser has no conception of what he is buying.
In Canada we have developed an effective method of inspection and grading with respect to primary products and farm commodities, but so far we have done little that has been effective with respect to manufactured products. For instance, under the Livestock and Livestock Products Act we have the inspection of stockyards, livestock, livestock products and poultry production. Under the same act we have inspection of hogs, carcass grading, grading of bacon for export, branding of beef, grading of lamb and mutton carcasses. We also have regulations respecting stockyards, the export of dairy cattle, the grading of unwashed fleece wool, dressed poultry, and the grading, branding and marketing of canned poultry. Under the Meat and Canned Foods Act we have inspection of meats, meat products, horse meat, fish and shellfish intended for canneries. Under the Dairy Industry Act we have inspection of milk, cream, condensed milk, evaporated milk, cheese, ice cream or any other article manufactured from milk or any imitation thereof. Under the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act we have regulations for the grading and inspection of fruits, vegetables and honey. Under the Meat and Canned Foods Act we have regulations for the grading and inspection of canned fruits and vegetables. Under the Maple Products Industry Act we have regulations for the grading and inspection of maple products. Under the Seeds Act, 1937, we have regulations for the grading and inspection of seeds. Under the Feeding Stuffs Act, 1937, we have regulations for the branding and inspection of feeds manufactured for consumption by livestock. Under the Inspection and Sale Act, 1938, we have regulations for the grading and inspection of flax fibres. Under the Hay and Straw Inspection Act, 1933, we have regulations for certain standards and inspection. Under the Fertilizers Act we have regulations covering the content of fertilizers and for the inspection of the same. Under the Pest Control Products Act we have regulations for certain standards and provisions for commodities coming under this act. Lumber is also sold according to grades and subject to inspection previous to sale, particularly for export.
I want to emphasize again how far we have developed the inspection and grading of

primary and agricultural products, as compared with the inspection, grading and labelling of manufactured products. I find that the Food and Drugs Act is administered by the Department of National Health and Welfare. This service is supposed to protect the public's pocketbook by assuring the customer that he will receive what he believes he is purchasing in the way of food and drugs.
In the annual report of the Department of National Health and Welfare dated March 31, 1948, it is stated that the inspection service of this department reviewed 7,961 radio programs, 2,137 labels and 395 pieces of advertising material. According to the report, after all this examination one prosecution was launched and a conviction obtained. During the same period in the United States, under similar but more advanced legislation, approximately 20,000 definite violations of the law were determined. I think that in itself, Mr. Speaker, is evidence that in this country we lag behind the United States with respect to legislation of this type.
I find also that the Department of National Health and Welfare has a laboratory service which has given some consideration to cosmetic chemistry. I find in this report they have given some study to the analysis of face powders, vanishing creams, and so on. A number of reports from the public regarding violations of the law were received, but apparently there have been no prosecutions to date.
The same department investigates pharmaceutical chemistry. The report says that the Winnipeg laboratory made a valuable survey of headache products including some 80 samples of these products collected throughout the territory. According to the report only 45 fully met the requirements, yet there is no evidence of any prosecutions. A noteworthy collection of ointments was analysed in Montreal, which revealed a considerable amount of misbranding.
Then, with respect to the administration of the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act which, I believe, is an important act, the report states that the annual production of patent medicines in Canada for the year 1945 amounted to $60,330,928. Now that is an amazing amount of the Canadian consumer's dollar which is being spent upon what a good many of the members of this house consider pure trash. I believe it is necessary for any government to do all it possibly can to protect the consumer.
Effective action along these lines, according to reports issued by the United States government, has been taken for a number of years but in Canada we have done very little. Under
National Trade Mark
the legislation existing in the United States, the federal trade commission has investigated hundreds of thousands of products and the question of labelling those products. According to the best evidence obtainable not very much of that sort of work has been undertaken in Canada. I could not obtain evidence of the sort I have mentioned in Canada, but in the United States there are some illustrations of the junk which is on the shelves of the stores. Many of these brands are in Canadian stores and should not be purchased by Canadian people without full knowledge of the facts.
I intend to give a few illustrations of the findings of the federal trade commission of the United States and others throughout the years concerning these commodities, many of which can be found for sale in Canadian stores. I shall deal with the subject under various heads. There are 7 brands of castile soap which, when analysed, were found to contain no olive oil at all, although it is supposed to be one of the basic contents of good soap. In the soap chips there was not sufficient naphtha to have any value as a cleansing agent, although according to the advertisements it is supposed to loosen, soften and dissolve dirt. The best soap can be sold at 20 cents a pound.
Then we come to drugs. I am taking the time of the house to put this matter before the government, because I believe it is important. What about Murine eyewash? You see it advertised quite often. Chemical analysis showed Murine to be essentially a solution of borax in water with a trace of berberin or some golden seal preparation. Furthermore, the formula was found to change from time to time. If you bought your own borax and mixed it with water, it is estimated you could make about a gallon of Murine for five cents. In the container in which it is sold it costs you $1 an ounce, $16 a pint, or $128 per gallon.
The next product with which I wish to deal is Doan's kidney pills. The government of the United States has declared that the claim of this nostrum to cure kidney disease is false and fraudulent, and the courts have upheld the ruling.
I know a good many people who are in the habit of purchasing Nuxated Iron. A dollar bottle of Nuxated Iron was found by the chemists of the American Medical Association to contain less than 2 J grains of iron. The claim that Nuxated Iron possesses great advantages over other forms of iron is the sheerest buncombe.
Then we come to this well-known mother's remedy, California syrup of figs. I know dozens of people who have purchased that

National Trade Mark
bread the way Hollywood has glorified the American girl. Man does not live by bread alone, but it is the foundation of our diet, and our sliced loaves of cotton batting are a weak foundation for anything.
What America needs is bread with crust to exercise the teeth and stick to the ribs, bread to strengthen the heart for the tasks which lie ahead.
I mention that, Mr. Speaker, because, in the application of this act and related acts, I think it is necessary that the government do everything possible to make certain in the first instance at least that essential foods, such as bread, are manufactured purely for the use of the Canadian public.
Before ending I just want to mention the question of barbed wire. It comes to my mind because I know hon. members know me to be a peasant farmer. I am not like one of these huge machine farmers on the prairies with his thousands of acres and his thousands of dollars and huge buildings. I am just a small fruit farmer, keeping a few head of stock, who has made his living not by sitting on a rubber-tired combine but by using a mattock, an axe and a saw, and who works with his hands. But just the same, I do use barbed wire to fence in my fields and my pasture. I think hon. gentlemen who are farmers on this side will agree with me when I say that the quality of barbed wire has deteriorated terribly since the war. Previous to the war we got a heavy grade of good barbed wire which would keep a bull out or in if it was properly stretched. For years now we have been buying an inferior grade. We cannot buy a good grade of barbed wire. You dare not stretch it beyond a certain tightness because it will snap. We have a poor quality of barbed wire in this country at this time, and it is sold at a high price. The government should give some consideration to making certain that when a farmer or anyone else buys a commodity such as barbed wire, which I give as an illustration, he will know that he is buying a quality commodity of a certain standard and of a certain value.
I wish to refer to roofing. A farmer often has to put a roof on the woodshed, on the granary, or on an outdoor building of some sort. Today you have no idea what you are buying. On one occasion I was purchasing roofing and I thought I was getting a high quality roofing. It was supposed to be four ply, or something of that sort. I said: "Give me the best; I want it to last as long as possible." I found out later that I could have got exactly the same roofing-one was red and the other was green-at about $2 a roll less. That is the sort of situation that ought to be corrected in this country. Farming people, working people and others should [Mr. Herridge.i
have some confidence in what they are purchasing. There must be, shall I say, a set of standards established with regard to the essential things required in the building of homes, in development of farms and for all consumer needs.
This bill, Mr. Speaker, if it is effectively enforced, means that science has gained another foothold in the fight against misinterpretations and fraud. I say "if effectively enforced". I do not expect to see sudden action in this connection, because I am quite sure it is going to take time to develop public understanding and procedures on the part of the department.
If this legislation is to be effective, not only must the government through the department administer the act and find procedures, but it must get the support of the Canadian people. It is not going to be effective, and cannot be effectively enforced, unless it receives the support of Canadian producers and Canadian consumers, the very active and intelligent support of the Canadian people.
In this connection there is a splendid opportunity for women's organizations, farm women's organizations, women's institutes, Imperial Order of the Daughters of the Empire, the Legion Auxiliary and so forth. Women are particularly fitted for this type of work and for keeping a watchful eye on this type of legislation. There is a great opportunity for women's organizations in this country to assist the government in the enforcement and in the development of this legislation. The same applies to trade unions. The workingmen of this country should be very interested in this type of legislation; so should the farm organizations. When they are aware of the possibilities of the further development of this type of legislation this government will receive the active support of the farmers, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and allied farm organizations in developing and administering this type of legislation. The same thing applies to co-operatives, and finally to the individual.
I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that a democracy is only as strong as the democracy that exists within it, and the democracy that exists within any country is finally determined by the willingness of the individual to accept some personal responsibility in the administration of the law and the development of our society.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I trust that, in the passing of this legislation and in the administration and enforcement of the act, public support will develop to the advantage of the Canadian people. I support this bill, Mr. Speaker, in the hope that the Canadian

papers generally will, as I said before, emulate the Christian Science Monitor and other very well-known American papers in effectively supporting the government in the development of this type of legislation. I trust also that it will receive the widespread support of all sections of the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support this bill, and I should like to make one or two brief observations. I think every party in this house can compliment the government on introducing the bill, because it is long past due. The protection which it affords is long past due. I suggest to the minister that there should be a provision requiring a manufacturer or producer who asks for a brand to pay fair wages to the workers who produce the article for which the brand is wanted. I believe we should make quite sure that it is produced under the best working conditions possible and, if possible, certified by a trade union that the contents of the package have been produced by fair wages, and fair living and working conditions. I make that suggestion because I think such a requirement should be insisted upon before any brand is given to any firm.
An article can sometimes qualify for the brand when the conditions under which the article was produced could not qualify under the decent standards of living that we are trying to establish in this country. That was amply demonstrated some years ago during an investigation into the working conditions in some of our industries, particularly the clothing industry, and so on. It was proved that the article was good, but the conditions of the people producing the article were deplorable and were condemned wholeheartedly by the findings of that commission. I merely make that remark because I understand another speaker is to follow me and deal with that phase of the question.

One other thing I suggest is that the container on which the trade-mark appears shall not be either used or filled again by any unauthorized person. In the part of the country from which I come, the Okanagan valley, we have a product that I have no doubt will qualify for the national trademark. In the meantime we have the O.K. brand which is pretty well equivalent to what any other government brand would be. It is well known everywhere that the packages that bear this name are often re-used for inferior quality goods. As a matter of fact, if you care to go down to Elgin street you will find boxes labelled "O.K. Brand Peaches", the very best grown in the Okanagan, filled with apples and tomatoes of rather low grade. That is what I refer to. Therefore, right here in Ottawa, there are people transgressing the method employed by a reputable firm to turn out a good product that they can guarantee. Naturally they expect support from the retailers and consumers in general. The same can be said of many other commodities. I could mention several. It happened especially during the war when certain commodities were in short supply. I refer particularly to a popular sauce from England, which I presume could be purchased in Canada. I saw the container, the bottle in which it originally came to Canada, used over and over again by restaurants all across the dominion. They used the brand name of that particular sauce for a concoction made in their own kitchens, one which was very inferior in quality. So that the label, in that sense, did not mean a great deal.
It is important to protect those people who conscientiously try to live up to the standards which we seek to impose upon them by this bill. When one has done that, and then is victimized through carelessness in the operation of the act, either in the retail or consumer end, we are at fault. I would suggest that there be inserted in the act a section stating that where a container has been used for an article complying with a national standard, and such container is emptied, it be destroyed or disfigured in such a way that it cannot be used again for a similar commodity and so definitely mislead the consuming public.
I would impress upon the minister the responsibility of printers in connection with the supplying of labels. The printing and distribution of labels should be carefully checked. I know that most firms printing labels are reputable, and will sell such labels only to those persons qualified to purchase them. Before a label can be sold to any firm, the firm purchasing such label should produce definite proof that it has the approval

National Trade Mark
of the government to make the purchase. I say this because during the war one could purchase scotch or rye with almost any label one wished; it was the same bottle, but the label was changed to suit the fancy of the customer.
This has been done in connection with other commodities. Men could be found who were willing to print labels by the thousand for sale to anyone. This included even the printing of government seals in British Columbia. Such labels have been sold to people who bootlegged products of inferior quality under the guise of approval by the provincial government.
Firms purchasing labels should give some definite proof to the printer that they are entitled to such labels. I know this would be difficult to do, because people who print the type of labels to which I have just referred usually do it surreptitiously, and are hard to find. They will operate in basements, or quarters of that kind. I would suggest that labels should be made definitely clear and specific as to the contents of the boxes, bottles or cartons on which they appear. The printing on the label which appears on the container of an article offered for sale should not be so small that the average purchaser cannot read it, or have to use a magnifying glass to see the print. Containers should be clearly marked as to their contents; they should be marked in such a way that anyone looking at a bottle or any other type of container may know the contents without difficulty.
May I next refer to bedding, which I imagine would come under a provision of this kind. For some time we in British Columbia have sought a pure-bedding act. Thus far we have not got it, with the result that bedding unfit for use is being sold in Canada. Some years ago-and not many years at that-the state of Washington passed a pure-bedding law whereby old mattresses could not be resold in any shape or form, with the result that dealers in bedding who usually made some allowance for old mattresses no longer had any use for them. The result was that they had an accumulation of these old mattresses which they shipped to Vancouver. In Vancouver the covers were ripped off and the contents pieced together- not cleaned. The mattresses were recovered with new ticking and sold in Vancouver and other points in British Columbia as new bedding. I know this to be an actual fact.
We should have a strict regulation which would refer particularly to bedding, because I am sure many diseases can be transmitted through the use of uncleaned bedding of this kind, whether it be in the form of mattresses, blankets or other bed coverings. Mattresses

should be clearly stamped indicating that the contents are brand new and made according to the specifications required to secure a Canada standard label. Naturally only the best and most reputable firms could secure that brand. I will say however that many firms today using cotton in its raw form, whether in chesterfields or bedding, have adopted a system of their own whereby they affix a label stating that the contents are 100 per cent pure, clean and new. This however is done purely of their own volition.
In my view the act should make provision for the control of advertising. As my colleague from Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) has just shown, advertising can be ridiculous and fantastic. These fantastic claims continue to be made regarding many commodities one can think of. So clever are the advertisements that their producers are actually in higher brackets of pay than are the producers of the article the advertising agent seeks to sell. The agent is regarded as the more clever.
An article may be all that is desired, it may be pure and come up to all the required specifications; but from the standpoint of selling that is not enough. It must be glamourized; and for its sale one must secure the services of a man who can, as my colleague says, bring Hollywood into the set-up, and sell something that is not exactly what it is meant to be. Any firm practising wrong advertising or making fantastic claims, whether the product meets with specifications or not, should immediately lose its privilege of having the brand assigned to it. This must be stopped, whether it applies to food products, face creams, toilet products or any other articles. It does not matter what the product may be; the practice of truth in advertising must some day prevail, and this could be a first step in demanding that all who receive labels must conform to fair trade practices in their advertising, particularly that appearing in popular magazines.
One can read these advertisements in magazines today where absurd claims are made. Some time ago in England some of the prominent sections of the press, including Punch and the Daily Mirror, took steps in this direction. The Daily Mirror indicated that it would not accept an advertisement for their paper which they themselves could not back up 100 per cent. For that purpose they had their own staff, which scrutinized every advertisement offered to their paper. If it met with their approval, after investigation, the advertiser was given the privilege of continued advertising.

I would appeal to the press of this country to co-operate with the department in making this bill a successful effort to make Canadian products known throughout the world for what they are stated to be on the labels, the contents being of best quality.

Mr. Speaker, I have only two brief observations to make, which will not take long. First I feel the government should be assured from all sides of the house that it will have the support of the people of Canada in pushing the use of the trade-mark "Canada standard" as provided by this bill. When the parliamentary assistant was introducing the measure some of us felt it was too bad he could not go a little further in making these standards more compulsory. I think I know the reason, namely, the difficulty we encounter as to provincial and federal jurisdiction under the British North America Act. I take it, however, the bill is based upon the premise that, if the federal government is going to accord to certain producers of goods the right to use a federal trade-mark, the federal government has the right to indicate the standards that must be met in order to use that trade-mark. If that is the case, then the course for the government to follow, under the constitutional division of powers as it now stands, is to popularize and push this trade-mark for all it is worth. It would seem to me, as one product after another meets the standard laid down and is able to use the letters "C.S.", that the people of Canada would be encouraged to want goods that have that particular mark on them, and in turn that would encourage the producers of other goods to try to meet these standards as well.
I remind the government that during the war under the wartime prices and trade board there was what was called, I believe, a bureau of standards. Under price control it became necessary to see to it that the purpose of price control was not defeated by the quality of goods being allowed to deteriorate. Therefore a bureau of standards was set up, and I am sure members of the government know as well as we do that the women of Canada in particular were most grateful for it. They liked the idea, and they came to feel during the war that, whatever else they might have to complain about, when they bought goods with a W.P.T.B. ticket on them they knew there was some supervision and inspection as to the standard of quality of the particular article. I am sure there is widespread support for the principle of the bill, for the institution of this trade-mark, and I hope that it will be pushed by the department. Some improvements have been
National Trade Mark
made in the new bill compared with the previous legislation. It seems to me it has been made more workable, and I hope that it will not be a measure, as the old one was, that will be more or less buried and become inoperative.
The other thing I should like to say has already been referred to by my colleague, the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Jones). In this connection I may say to the minister that I should like to offer an amendment to one of the clauses of his bill when we get into committee. I think it will be in order for me to mention it now in the hope that he will have at least that long to think it over, and be able to accept the amendment I propose to make when we reach the committee stage. As the hon. member for Yale has said, it does seem that, when we give the good name of Canada to products that are produced for sale either within or without Canada, we should be sure that that good name does not cover up poor working conditions. It should be a guarantee that, in addition to the goods meeting certain qualifications and standards, the workers who have been employed in producing them have been paid decent wages and have worked under decent conditions. As a matter of fact, it would seem to me that manufacturers would want it that way. Otherwise it would be possible for one manufacturer, who was paying poorer wages, to get the label or trade-mark by keeping up the quality of his goods when another manufacturer who was paying better wages might not be able to get it.
In case anybody raises the constitutional question, it seems to me that the answer is fairly simple. These working conditions would be put on the same basis as the other conditions set out in the bill. The federal government is not laying down mandatory provisions so far as standards of goods are concerned. They are simply saying: Here is our trade-mark; we cannot compel you to meet these conditions but if you want our trade-mark these are the conditions you must meet. I submit if the federal government has the power to do that so far as the standards and qualities of goods are concerned, it has the right to do the same thing with respect to labour conditions. As the British North America Act is now being interpreted, the federal government claims it has no right to invade the provincial field and say that such-and-such must be the general labour conditions, but the federal government has the right, just the same as with the other phases of this matter, to say that so far as this federal trade-mark is concerned we are not giving it unless,

(f)	and (g) are negative in character, and it seemed to me that was where it should go. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Cape Breton South:
That clause 4, subclause (1), of Bill 133, be amended by inserting therein after paragraph (e) a new paragraph (ee) to read as follows:

subtopic: APPLICATION TO COMMODITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have every sympathy with the objectives which this amendment is trying to attain, but it seems to me that there would be real difficulty in applying anything of this nature in determining a Canada standard. I believe my hon. friend has put his finger on the essential point when he said that the best label to protect working conditions is the union label. To substitute anything else for the union label would, I believe, meet with serious objection from the labour unions. No doubt the hon. member is aware of the fact that the union label is a bargaining weapon, and a valuable privilege granted by labour unions under certain conditions. I believe that is one objection.
Another objection would be that this would cut across provincial jurisdiction. In effect, it asks us to set a minimum wage and minimum working conditions on a national scale for industries using the "Canada standard" label. I doubt if this government would have the right to do so. Perhaps the Minister of Labour is able to discuss this more intelligently than I can.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO COMMODITIES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend has mentioned the union label. Many years ago in Hamilton I used to be a delegate to the union label league, and I think I know something about union labels. Is there a union label on the suit my hon. friend is wearing at the moment?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: APPLICATION TO COMMODITIES
speechtext: That's right, and I have my union card in my pocket.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO COMMODITIES
speechtext: I am talking about union labels. There is a union label on my coat, my vest and my pants.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO COMMODITIES
speechtext: Go on.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO COMMODITIES
speechtext:
I understand trade unions and I know that they are jealous of their labels. The painters have a label; the cigar makers have a label; the printers certainly have a label; the lithographers have a label,

and the die stampers. There are over a hundred labels which are given protection by a statute. I believe that statute was introduced some years ago by a Liberal government. I knew some of the prime movers of that statute, and it is rather revealing to look at it. It says:
No union label registered by any labour union may be assigned by any other process of law or otherwise.
That is section 15, subsection 3, of chapter 201, an act respecting Trade Marks and Industrial Design. As the Minister of Trade and Commerce said, the union label is a bargaining point. It is of use to the trade unions in ensuring good working conditions. I believe my hon. friend was in the printing trade and I am sure he will agree with me when I say that the printers are jealous of their label. So are all other trade unions. I know when I go to get a haircut-I have not much hair -the first thing I do is to look for the union label in the shop. It is a guarantee that the employees are getting good working conditions.
I believe that that is far better than any legislation. The use of this label is not mandatory. I do not take second place to anyone in this House of Commons in my advocacy of good working conditions, but if this amendment were adopted it might create hardships for one section of an industry. Take the canning industry, for instance, with all its ramifications from the production of the base metal to the completion of the cans and putting the contents in the can. As my hon. friend is aware, there are many union labels carried on cans and articles of that description.
I say this sincerely to the hon. member, that he is defeating his own purpose. I am not questioning his sincerity, but he is defeating his own purpose by amending this particular bill in that manner without consultation with some of the labour organizations in this country. I cannot recall any resolution or any demand on the part of labour organizations for this particular type of legislation. By insisting upon this amendment, one may be creating hardship for some well-organized trade that enjoyed good working conditions within an industry. Perhaps in some other industry that was not the case. Organization is the answer to that.
I have never been a great believer in setting minimum wages by law except to protect young people and women engaged in industry. Experience has taught us that when minimum wages are created by law the minimum becomes the maximum. If my friend looks across this country he may find some exceptions, but as a rule it is the

case. In the United States, the minimum wage was recently raised from 40 cents to 75 cents per hour in industries under the jurisdiction of the federal government. It is an indication that there must have been a good many people working at substandard rates in the interim between the establishment of the 40 cent per hour minimum and the 75 cent per hour minimum.
I join with the Minister of Trade and Commerce in saying I do not think you would be rendering a service to the trade union organizations of this country by adopting this amendment. So far as I am concerned, I would prefer the union label. I believe it is an indication that the men are free men and are not being dominated by a government. They have negotiated agreements and I think that is the proper way relations between employers and employees should be conducted, particularly in view of the fact there has been an enormous growth in trade unions in Canada during the last ten years.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO COMMODITIES
speechtext:
I believe both the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Labour are under a misapprehension. If the union label-in other words trade union conditions-is the best proof of the existence of a standard, you do not need to go any further; you have exactly what you want. As I understand it, this is voluntary legislation. The provisions of the bill are not mandatory; that is, we are not stepping in and telling manufacturers that they must do so-and-so. We are merely saying that if you produce a product of a certain quality, the Dominion of Canada will put on that product the hallmark, or whatever mark you call it, of quality "Canada standard"; but the product itself must first of all be of the required quality. If it is not, we have no power under this bill to compel producers or manufacturers to produce a product of the standard of quality that will receive the trade-mark. We contend that the quality may be good and may be of such a standard as to merit this trade-mark quality, but, at the same time, it may be produced under sweated labour conditions. If there is a trade union in the industry where the product is produced, we would assume that that was sufficient proof that it was not produced under sweated conditions.
We carry the same principle into government contracts through the fair wage policy; that is the wage that is accepted in the particular locality. But you might indeed go a little further than that. The Minister of Labour said that he was opposed to minimum wages. But a minimum wage is only required in industries in which the workers
National Trade Mark
are not organized. I know that for years the trade union movement did oppose minimum wages. In 1931, in the convention in Vancouver, the American Federation of Labor went on record as being opposed to unemployment insurance.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO COMMODITIES
speechtext: I was there.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO COMMODITIES
speechtext: They were foolishly trying to protect the trade union movement. In the old country the trade union movement for years was opposed to family allowances. I am well aware of the background of those fears. But all of the things I mentioned are now accepted by intelligent trade unionists everywhere as being of assistance in maintaining high standards of living and are not a detriment to trade unionism. I quite admit that there may be difficulty in finding a proper wording for a clause of this kind, but I believe that, if we accept the principle of it, it can be found.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO COMMODITIES
speechtext:
I think it is rather unfortunate that the Minister of Trade and Commerce did not discuss with the Minister of Labour the drafting of this bill. If I were Minister of Labour and Canada was preparing to adopt a bill of this nature, I think it would be my responsibility in the field of labour to see that those who produced the goods were also taken care of. I think the minister is in reverse in the statement he has made in this matter.
You cannot produce quality goods under sweat-shop conditions. I have no doubt that the hosiery industry, which is a low-paid industry and somewhat unorganized, can produce silk stockings and that kind of thing, and have them meet the standards that may be laid down. No standards are laid down in this act. It merely says that the research council will prepare specifications and standards. They may be able to meet the standards laid down by the research council; but I think one of the first things which should be done, before we put our trademark on any commodity that we are marketing in this country is to see to it that the people who actually produce that commodity are at least getting a fair break in the matter of wages and conditions.
This business of bringing the trade union label into the question is completely irrelevant to this bill. It has not anything to do with it. It is a good yardstick as to whether goods are quality goods or not and that conditions are fair and reasonable in any industry where the workers are organized and are bargaining. But we must not forget that only about 25 per cent of the workers of this country are eligible for membership in a union. The other 75 per cent will be

National Trade Mark
producing most of the goods that we are going to label and say meet the standards laid down by the research council and later adopted, I suppose, by this house. Seventy-five per cent of the people who actually produce the goods are not in a position to protect themselves with regard to a union label.
This measure will not be opposed by any trade unionist in this country if he has any sense, simply because this action in protecting the public, by bringing our commodities up to standard, will assist in the unionization of plants, in my opinion; and that is something that is badly needed at this time. I do not see any reason in the world why the minister cannot write in the clause suggested here, because it does not mean that you must go out and start to organize the workers of this country. It means that you are going to do exactly the same thing for the man who works in the plant and produces the goods as you are going to do for the manufacturer-that is, the decent manufacturer-who wants to produce quality goods. The bill merely states that you are simply going to lay down certain requirements and specifications for his goods. That is going to protect him against the fellow that wants to sell inferior goods. At the same time, if you add this clause (ee), you merely say that we are going to probe the possibility also of decent working conditions, hours of labour and wages in the plants and factories whose goods carry the trademark of Canada. There is no reason why that cannot be done. It does not interfere with anyone. It does not mean that you are going to do it overnight, because it is going to take some considerable time to build up in this country a standard product that is recognized even by our own people. I think both things go hand in hand, because you cannot get, under sweat-shop conditions, the kind of goods that you can put your O.K. on.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO COMMODITIES
speechtext:
I do not quite like this amendment because I feel that it may result in a form of discrimination. It reads as follows:
(ee) prescribing the rates of pay, hours of work, and other working conditions, under which commodities, packages or containers shall be produced if the national trade mark is applied thereto.
What would be the result in a canning factory if, in order to pay these rates of wages and maintain certain hours of labour, they felt that they could not maintain the price at which the commodity should be sold? The result would be that they would start to chisel on the primary producer who was supplying it with the commodities to put in

those packages. If you put that provision in there, you should also put in: "And shall prescribe the price paid for the products contained in those packages". Therefore, unless that proviso is put in, I would not be prepared to support the amendment. Otherwise, it would just mean discrimination against the primary producer.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO COMMODITIES
speechtext:
I think the hon. member for Acadia has misinterpreted the amendment. The amendment states, as he has read: prescribing the rates of pay, hours of work, and other working conditions, under which commodities, packages or containers shall be produced if the national trade mark is applied thereto.
The tomatoes and corn that go into the can are commodities; and if this amendment were applied, it could be applied to the minimum price, as meaning the minimum price for the agricultural product that went into the can, as well as to the hours and conditions of the labourer who produces the can.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO COMMODITIES
speechtext: No. I must correct my hon. friend there. The mark "Canada standard" on a package means that the commodity itself is standard, but it does not necessarily mean that the fruit, before it was canned, was standard. If we accepted this amendment my hon. friend would hardly wish to take it back into all the components that go into the finished article. I think that would be quite impossible. In any event, what he is asking is that the government prescribe rates of pay. That means we would have to put in a coast to coast rate of pay for a given commodity. There are minimum wage laws in every province, and they are all different in some respect. I do not see how we could set a rate of pay for a commodity, and prescribe hours of work. How could we do that? British Columbia works a forty-hour week, and Ontario perhaps a forty-five or a forty-eight-hour week. How could we say that one would have the standard and the other could not? I think that by accepting the amendment we would make the act completely unenforceable. As the act is written today, if an article is found in the United Kingdom it can be tested, and the test checked against the specifications, and it either complies with the specifications or it does not. But if the article also had to be traced back to its origin and a determination made as to whether fair wages were paid we would have a wholly unworkable act. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I hope the committee will not accept the amendment.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: APPLICATION TO COMMODITIES
speechtext:
May I say that to prescribe rates of pay, hours of work, and other working conditions would not necessarily involve,

at the federal level, all the detail that the minister suggests. For example, it might be solved by simply requiring that the fair wage conditions in the various provinces be met before the label is granted. It might prescribe-and I would so urge-that in certain classes of goods the union label would be the only acceptable proof of proper working conditions. In other words, it does not have to be shown in terms of a wage rate for every class of employee right across the country; it could be done in general classifications. As a matter of fact, something similar to that happens in some of the provinces today where the fair wage legislation hinges in part on what the trade union rates are in a particular industry; and in industries not so well organized some detail is given.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that it is not as difficult to find a general formula for prescribing working conditions as it is to prescribe qualities and standards for all the different kinds and classes of things that may come under this legislation. The bill provides for that; I think my amendment is even more important. Frankly, I do not feel that the objection raised by the Minister of Trade and Commerce carries weight.
While I am on my feet may I say one word with respect to what the Minister of Labour had to say. He tried to make a comparison between this national trade-mark and the union label, and suggested that the union label was good enough and that we should not have the provision I ask for with respect to the national trade-mark. May I point out, as did the hon. member for Cape Breton South, that there are a lot of goods produced by workers who are either unorganized or are in fields in which the union label is not used. By this legislation what you are making possible is another label called "Canada standard", which sounds good, but which may not-and will not when my amendment carries-guarantee the conditions that the union label is guaranteeing on certain other goods. You will have people going into stores in Canada and buying goods and feeling satisfied with them because they have got the "Canada standard" label on them. People will be asked if they have bought union label goods. They will say: "Yes, I have. I have it here; it has 'C.S.' on it." It will not be worth what the union label is worth, and it will actually be a detriment to the trade union movement in this country to have another label competing with the trade union label, a government label which will not be worth half what the trade union label is worth. I am saying the way to make
National Trade Mark
this "Canada standard" label worth something is to put this kind of clause into the bill and leave it, as the clause says, to the governor in council to work out the proper regulations.

speechtext: May I refer to one point? You do not have to use this label to begin with. Let us take the condition of the organized people in industry at the moment. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext: I laughed because I thought the minister was punning.

speechtext: No, I am not. I am trying to be sensible.

speechtext: There is no harm in trying.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO COMMODITIES
speechtext: I think I have as much experience with these things as the average member in the house, especially in connection with minimum wage laws. As hon. members know, I was chairman of the Ontario executive board of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada seven years. Do you want the standard to apply to sugar from the West Indies, for instance? I refer to the people who are interested in the great international movements. Take many other things that enter into it. Some of the things that we are speaking about are basic. I believe the best form of protection is an organization. You can have all the laws in the world so far as I am concerned; when you get the workers organized that is the yardstick of progress. The hon. member for Vancouver East is a member of a street railway union. It would have been just too bad for these street railway men if they had to put this kind of label on the streetcar to see whether a person rode on it or not. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is a member of the printers' union. It would have been just too bad if the printers had to use this kind of legislation to see that they got good working conditions. It would have been just too bad for the miners of the hon. member for Cape Breton South if they had to lean on legislation of this kind. And so on right across the board. As I said before, for defenceless people, for women and young people, it is all right, but I would prefer straight negotiation for grown-up people. The union label is superior to any minimum wage law under the canopy of heaven.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: APPLICATION TO COMMODITIES

This bill makes it possible for the label "Canada standard" to be put on packages. The minister spoke to me as a printer. As a printer I want the union label on packages.

Just a word; I would not like to see this amendment pass without saying something on it. No matter what the intent of the amendment is it is the wording that you have to decide on. To start with, I do not think we should try to create an advantage for one class of citizens to the disadvantage of another class. When you look at the amendment closely you find that it says:
Prescribing the rates of pay, hours of work, and other working conditions, under which commodities, packages, or containers shall be produced if the national trade mark is applied thereto.
It is true that it speaks of commodities, but the working conditions attached to it are three, namely, rates of pay, hours of work, and working conditions. I am all for giving the workingman the advantage of the situation. I want to see him have the highest possible standard of living; but under this amendment, as the hon. member for Acadia said, you can maintain wages, rates of pay, as it is called, the hours of work and the other working conditions. You can keep these at a high level to the detriment of the man who produces the raw materials. I would be most hesitant about passing this in its present form. If the sponsor of the amendment can change it so as to give all parties connected with the production of a product and its processing the advantage which he hopes, then I would be only too pleased to support it. But I can see very clearly that the agriculturist, for instance, who produces garden produce such as peas, corn and the like which go into the manufacture of commodities put in cans, upon which labels are placed, has absolutely no protection. In fact it may work out very much to his disadvantage in the long run. So, when it comes to placing one class against another, I think it is poor legislation. I am of the opinion that labourers throughout the country would view it that way. I cannot support it in its present form.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I deal first with what the hon. member for Bow River has said. He still clings to the old-fashioned idea that in order that farmers may prosper the industrialist worker must be kept on a low wage.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO COMMODITIES
speechtext: No, no, no.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO COMMODITIES
speechtext:
There was never a more fallacious argument than that. The farmer

does not sell his products to other farmers. He sells his products to city people, the industrial workers. If the industrial worker does not get a wage that enables him to buy the things the farmer produces, then the farmer will be poor.
Now for the Minister of Labour; he can draw more red herrings across the trail than any other person I ever met in my life. He talks about the great advantages of unions, organized labour, and he mentions the organization to which I belong, the street railway-men's union. He has referred to the printers' union, and to various other unions. But all of the labour unions he referred to are in relatively protected industries, in industries in which it is easy for the workers to organize. The people who need protection are not the people who can protect themselves, but those who cannot protect themselves. That is what we are trying to do by this amendment.
It is very easy for the skilled workers, or the workers in industry where there is a virtual monopoly, such as in street railway transportation, to organize. I remember at one time hearing the president of the company for which I worked say that we got good conditions partly because the company's own condition was so precarious that they could not afford a struggle with the union. That is a fact.
What we want is not that those who are strong should maintain good conditions for themselves, but that we make sure that those who cannot maintain good conditions for themselves, because of their weakness, will be protected. It is for that purpose that the amendment is moved. As I said before, there may be some difficulty in wording it so that it will meet the intended purpose; but that should not be beyond the ingenuity of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and his most efficient staff.
